title: Workspaces orphaned by a stale id: Dispose must reclaim by identity, not by bookkeeping
description:
Workspaces survive their tick and become unreachable: the tick is CLOSED, the
manifest that named the workspace is GONE, the workspace and its git worktree
are still live, and the workspace's tick tokens are missing — so nothing can
find it by tick id ever again. Only a human reading a sidebar notices.

Observed 2026-09-10 in the canonify repo (a different epic, same substrate):
workspaces wP5 j5s, wP6 0i9, wP7 226, wP8 hf1, wP9 3i5, wPA 15e, wPB fw3 all
alive with worktrees under ~/.herdr/worktrees/canonify/tick-*, all with
`tokens: {}` in `herdr workspace list`, all with their tick CLOSED and NO
manifest under `.tick/logs/herd/*/`. The one workspace that still carries
`TICK=we9` is the one whose tick is still in_progress.

ticks' own cleanup is careful and is probably NOT the bug: it removes the
manifest LAST so an incomplete teardown is retryable, it re-checks liveness next
to the destructive step rather than at run start, and it refuses when herdr will
not answer. Two of its behaviours combine badly with a herdr RESTART, which is
the likely trigger — herdr went 0.8.2 to 0.9.0 (protocol 20 to 22) in this
window:

1. `planFor` notes "manifest records no workspace id — nothing to remove in
   herdr" and proceeds to remove the manifest anyway.
2. `apply` treats `workspace_not_found` from worktree.remove as SUCCESS — which
   is right when the workspace is genuinely gone, and wrong when the id in the
   manifest is merely STALE. Either way the manifest is then removed, and the
   real workspace, now under an id nothing records, is unreachable.

Workspace tokens are herdr-side metadata (set through pane/workspace
report_metadata), so a restart that loses them removes the last independent way
to re-derive the mapping.

## Why this belongs in Phase 2

ticfac's executor owns Dispose, and Phase 1 already established the two
principles this needs. Attempts are ADOPTED BY TICK ID rather than by a
remembered handle, and the reconciler PRUNES missing worktrees at startup. The
herdr executor must do the equivalent for workspaces, or the same leak arrives
in ticfac with the same shape.

Do:
- Dispose must be idempotent AND identity-based: given a tick and an attempt it
  must be able to find the workspace even when the recorded id is stale, by
  asking herdr what exists rather than trusting bookkeeping. A workspace whose
  worktree path names the tick is evidence; so is a branch.
- Do NOT treat `workspace_not_found` as proof of teardown when the id could be
  stale. Distinguish "this workspace is gone" from "this id is unknown", and
  refuse rather than record success on the second — the same fail-closed rule
  tick x6j applies to substrate answers generally.
- Reclamation at startup: a run should be able to list herdr workspaces whose
  tick belongs to this epic and whose tick is CLOSED, and report them. Removal
  is destructive, so report first; only remove what the operator or a declared
  policy authorises.
- Record the workspace id in provenance alongside the herdr protocol and server
  version (tick d9m), so a stale id can be recognised as stale rather than
  guessed at.

Note the interaction with resume-across-an-upgrade, which d9m and x6j already
own: this is the same hazard seen from the disposal end rather than the dispatch
end. A herdr restart is exactly when both bite.

## The second orphan shape: the pointer dies with the thing it points at

Observed again on 2026-09-10, on this epic's own wave 1. Tearing down 579, 8ug
and p4s each reported:

    remove-manifest  .tick/logs/herd/av8/<tick>.json
    note  agent tick-<id> is still live (status idle) on a merged branch —
          worktree.remove tears it down with the workspace

The manifest is the ONLY durable pointer from a tick to its workspace, and it is
removed as part of the same operation that removes the workspace. ticks orders
this as carefully as it can — the manifest goes LAST, so an incomplete teardown
is retryable — but the window is real: interrupt after the manifest is gone and
before the workspace is, or hand it a workspace id that a herdr restart made
stale, and nothing can ever name that workspace again. That is exactly how the
seven canonify orphans were made. These three completed cleanly, so no leak
here; the shape is the same.

ticfac starts from a better position and must not give it up. Phase 1's rule is
that cleanup is LAST, after the close — "a cleanup before the close throws away
the only copy of what was closed" — and its durable records live in `.ticfac/`
ON THE INTEGRATION BRANCH, pushed to origin, rather than in a local file that
teardown deletes.

So, in addition to the reclamation above:

- **The durable pointer must outlive the teardown.** Whatever identifies the
  workspace must be a record on the integration branch, not a local file, and
  it must not be removed as a step of the teardown it describes. Removing it is
  the LAST thing, after the workspace is provably gone, or it is not removed at
  all and disposal is simply idempotent.
- **An interrupted teardown must be resumable.** Kill the run between any two
  steps of Dispose and the next run must find the workspace from durable state
  and finish the job — not shrug because the pointer is gone. A test that kills
  disposal midway and asserts the next run completes it is the one that settles
  this.
- **"Still live on a merged branch" is a normal state, not a warning to step
  around.** All three of ours reported it. Disposal must handle a live agent on
  merged work as an ordinary case with a defined order (revoke, stop, remove),
  which is Phase 1's A1 rule, rather than as an edge worth a note.
notes: 2026-09-10 13:04 - Distinction that matters for the fix, checked in code: these three were NOT orphans, they were UNCOLLECTED. Under the tk herd ritual, cleanup is a manual orchestrator step — nothing reaps a finished worker's workspace on its own, so a workspace sits until somebody runs 'tk herd cleanup <id> --apply'. Under ticfac's reconciler it is already automatic and correctly ordered: processTick ends with r.cleanUp after the close (dispatch.go:194-196, 'Cleanup is LAST, and only after the close'), and rolejob.go does the same on both its close paths. So Phase 2 inherits the reaper it needs; what it must not inherit is the manual-step model, and what it must add is the reclamation for the case where the automatic path was interrupted or the recorded id went stale.
acceptance_criteria: Dispose finds and tears down a workspace whose recorded id is stale, by asking herdr what exists rather than trusting the manifest; a test drives disposal against a changed workspace id and asserts the workspace is actually gone. workspace_not_found is no longer recorded as successful teardown when the id may be stale: 'this workspace is gone' and 'this id is unknown' are distinguishable and the second refuses. A run can list and report herdr workspaces belonging to this epic whose tick is closed, without removing anything unless authorised. The workspace id is recorded in provenance alongside the herdr protocol and server version. go test -short -timeout 45m ./... green (make test-short). The record that identifies a workspace is durable on the integration branch rather than a local file, and is never removed as a step of the teardown it describes: it goes last, after the workspace is provably gone, or disposal is idempotent and it is not removed at all. An interrupted teardown is resumable, proven by a test that kills disposal between steps and asserts the next run finds the workspace from durable state and completes it. A live agent on a merged branch is an ordinary disposal case with a defined order, not a special note.
